graphics.title: Seeing a result is not explaining it
graphics.alt: A bus has a red display showing a 12-minute delay. That is an observation. A supplied engineering note says past journeys fitted the delay model; that is evidence about its mechanism.

graphics.title: Who or what makes this decision?
graphics.alt: A remote-controlled car follows human commands, a motion lamp follows a written rule, and a trained photo sorter applies a learned model. A product can combine mechanisms. AI also includes symbolic reasoning.

graphics.title: One bus display. Three different decisions.
graphics.alt: Three separate rows trace the bus estimate, display colour and driver override. The fitted model estimates 12 minutes; the written greater-than-10 rule makes the display red; the driver can choose ROUTE CLOSED.

graphics.title: Learn first. Predict later.
graphics.alt: Earlier weather records are used to fit a model. Later, new measurements are passed to that fitted model to obtain a 70 percent rain forecast. It is an estimate, not a guarantee.

graphics.title: Change the rule. Keep the forecast.
graphics.alt: With a 70 percent rain forecast, a 60 percent-or-more rule displays TAKE ONE. An 80 percent-or-more rule does not trigger that message. Only the boundary changed; the fitted model and forecast did not.

graphics.title: “Not enough information” is a useful answer
graphics.alt: An unspecified smart robot vacuum moves and cleans, but its route mechanism is unknown. Ask for evidence of human commands, written rules or model fitting, and allow combinations. Apply this reasoning to a classroom sorter.
